new_statements.rule_in_words: Waboda is described as having a 'complex stress system with rhythm patterns' (a family-wide characterisation) and, unlike the other Kiwaian languages, apparently no tone system; the position of word stress is not stated anywhere. The only positional remark in the literature is Wurm 1951 sec. 23 (snippet only, general 'Kiwai languages', from older sources): main stress in isolated words on the first syllable of disyllables and first or (more often) second syllable of trisyllables, shifting in connected speech to two or three syllables from the end of suffixed words 'on what principle cannot be said at present'; it is not shown to cover Wabuda.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (Wurm 1951 snippet notes 'stress markes on two or even three successive syllables' in the older sources, for the Kiwai languages generally).
new_statements.domain_note: Family-level generalisation over all Kiwaian languages plus a language-specific paragraph on Wabuda; Wabuda forms in the paper carry vowel-length marks (ko:bo 'water', ke:ra 'fire', sa:riki 'sun') but no stress marks. Wurm 1973 p.250 adds that 'stress features [are] yet to be studied in detail in North-Eastern Kiwai and the other Kiwaian languages'.
new_statements.identity_note: Wurm 1973 treats 'Wabuda' as one language (= Waboda, wabo1241) spoken on Wabuda Island, Aibinio Island, the left bank of the Fly and Dibiri Island; Ray 1923 and Riley & Ray 1930 note a Gesoa/Sagero variety 'with very different accent' (dialect sense, not word stress). Wurm 1951 (snippet) distinguishes a 'Wabuda Group' with island dialects incl. 'Wabuda proper'. No differently coded variety is involved.
